CARVEYANCE How It Works

How It Works · Headlights

Bright Idea

From oil lamps to computer-controlled beams, the headlight's story is also a story of glass lenses, disappearing eyes, yellow French nights and the clear covers that reshaped the face of the modern car.

By Diana Chambers · 23 minute read

There is a moment on every night drive when the streetlights give out and the car becomes the only light for miles. The dashboard settles into its glow, the trees close in, and everything you are about to meet arrives first as a shape at the edge of your beams. In that moment a headlight stops being a part number. It is the only promise the car can make about the road you haven't reached yet.

Long before automakers began considering how self-driving vehicles might communicate with people through light, headlights faced a more immediate challenge: helping a driver see the road after sunset. Their evolution has never been simply a race for brightness. It has involved controlling glare, improving reliability and finding room for lighting within changing vehicle designs, and the covers surrounding those lights have their own place in that history.

It has also, from the very beginning, been a matter of character. Headlights are the first thing we read on a car, the part of the front end that looks back at us. Children draw cars with eyes because cars have them. Designers know it, regulators have argued over it for a century, and anyone who has watched a pair of pop-ups blink awake in a parking garage has felt it.

1890s–1912When the Light Was a Flame

The first automobiles borrowed their light from the carriage. In the 1890s, cars carried oil lamps and then acetylene lamps, flame-based devices closer to coach lanterns than to anything we would call a headlight today. Acetylene was the clever one. Water dripped onto calcium carbide in a canister, the gas ran through a tube to the lamp, and the driver lit it with a match before setting off. It hissed, it smelled and it needed refilling, and on a dark country lane it was the most wonderful thing in the world, because without it the drive simply ended at sunset.

Electricity showed up almost at once and took years to win. The Electric Vehicle Company of Hartford, Connecticut, offered electric headlamps as an option on its Columbia Electric in 1898, which made sense for a car that already carried a large battery. Gasoline cars had no such luxury, since their electrics were barely strong enough to fire the spark plugs. Inventors tried everything anyway. In 1904 a small Massachusetts maker, Beverly, offered a headlight that turned with the front wheels, an idea that would be hailed as cutting-edge 44 years later on a Tucker.

The turning point came from Cadillac. The 1912 Model 30 combined electric starting with electric lighting, a single electrical system taking over 2 jobs that had always belonged to the driver: cranking the engine and lighting the way. Its headlights showed how a car's own electricity could take a chore off the driver's hands, and they set the pattern for every car since. From then on, night was something you drove into rather than something you waited out.

1915–1957Seeing Without Blinding

More usable light also made controlling its direction essential, and it brought the problem that has followed the headlight ever since. A beam strong enough to show you the road is strong enough to dazzle the person coming the other way, and on a 2-lane road at night those 2 people pass within a few feet of each other. Lighting engineers went after it early. HELLA's timeline records a low-beam development in 1915, and in 1925 Osram unveiled the Bilux in Berlin, the first bulb with 2 filaments, one for the low beam and one for the high beam, inside a single glass envelope. Dimming your lights soon moved to a button on the floor, where American drivers would stamp on it with their left foot for the next half century.

General Motors decided the driver shouldn't have to remember at all. In 1952 its Guide Lamp division offered the Autronic Eye on Cadillacs and Oldsmobiles, a phototube on top of the dashboard that watched for oncoming headlights and dropped your high beams before you had noticed them. It cost $53.36 (about $670 in 2026 money), and GM sold it as "an eye that is faster than your foot." It was the first car part ever designed to be polite on your behalf. Motor Trend, testing a 1953 Oldsmobile, found itself overriding the system more often than it would have liked, which is roughly how every automatic high beam has been reviewed since.

It was the first car part ever designed to be polite on your behalf.

Europe attacked the same problem through the shape of the beam. In 1957 HELLA's asymmetric low-beam headlamp was approved, a low beam that reached farther along the driver's own side of the road while staying low toward oncoming traffic. Look at any modern low beam on a garage wall and you'll still see that crooked edge, a little step up on the curb side. The central challenge was already recognizable, and it hasn't changed since: a headlight must help one person see without making it harder for someone else.

1940–19837 Inches, by Law

In America that challenge was handed to a standard. Starting with the 1940 model year, cars sold in the United States wore standardized 7-inch round sealed-beam headlamps, the result of an effort by state motor vehicle administrators and the industry to bring some order to headlighting. A sealed beam fused the filament, the reflector and the glass lens into a single unit. When it failed you replaced the whole thing, at any gas station in the country, and the fluted glass on its face did real optical work, bending the light into its pattern. The lens was the lamp's protective face and part of its brain at the same time.

It was sensible, cheap and fair, and it gave 4 decades of American cars the same eyes. Designers could set them closer together or farther apart, but they couldn't change their size or shape. The only real freedom was how many. In 1957 most states began to allow 4 smaller 5¾-inch lamps, and a few cars, among them the Nash Ambassador and the Cadillac Eldorado Brougham, were sold with nothing else even though quads weren't yet legal everywhere. By 1958 they were legal in all 48 states, and nearly every American car adopted them almost overnight.

Preston Tucker found out how strict those rules could be. His 1948 Tucker 48 carried a third headlight in the middle of its nose, the Cyclops Eye, which came on and turned with the steering once the wheel passed about 10 degrees, lighting the road around a corner instead of the ditch beyond it. At the time 17 states didn't allow more than 2 headlights, so Tucker supplied a cover to hide it. Only 51 Tuckers were built, and that cover may be the most American accessory ever offered: a lid over a good idea.

Europe, meanwhile, kept changing what was inside the lamp. In 1962 a consortium of European bulb and headlamp makers introduced the H1, the first halogen lamp for car headlights, and in 1971 the H4 put halogen low and high beams into a single bulb. Halogen lets a filament run hotter and whiter without blackening the glass, and it gave European drivers far more light than a sealed beam. Americans got halogen sealed beams only with the 1979 models, and the H1 itself wasn't approved in the US until 1997. For a generation of enthusiasts, swapping a car's sealed beams for European H4 lamps became a rite of ownership.

No car shows the gap more painfully than the Citroën SM. In Europe it wore 6 headlamps behind a single sheet of shaped glass, and the inner pair turned with the steering. In America swiveling lamps and glass covers were both off-limits, so the SM arrived with 4 fixed round lamps standing out in the open. It's the same car with a different face, and it tells you more about 1970s lighting law than any rulebook could. Its whole story is in Her Majesty Drives Herself.

1936–2004The Headlights That Closed Their Eyes

Alongside the changes in illumination came experiments in concealment. While Europe and America argued about light, a few designers decided the best headlight was one you couldn't see. The 1936 Cord 810, introduced at the New York auto show in November 1935, hid its lamps inside its sculpted fenders. They were modified Stinson aircraft landing lights, which was convenient, because E.L. Cord owned a majority of Stinson. The designer, Gordon Buehrig, wanted electric motors to raise them. Cost won, and the driver wound each lamp up with its own crank on the dashboard. Picture it: you stop at dusk, reach across the dash, turn 2 little handles, and the car opens its eyes.

Here, "headlight cover" means something different from a transparent lens: a movable panel or a retracting lamp hides the headlight while it's switched off, then exposes it for use. Federal rules published in 1968 explicitly addressed both movable covers and headlights that moved to hide themselves, which made hidden headlights a recognized category of equipment with requirements of their own. By then they had become the signature of every car that wanted to look fast standing still. The 1963 Corvette Sting Ray rotated its lamps out of its nose, and from then until 2004 every Corvette's headlights disappeared when they weren't needed. The 1962 Lotus Elan, the Lamborghini Miura with its eyelashes, the Lotus Esprit, the Porsche 928, the Mazda RX-7 and the first Miata all made a ceremony of waking up. For about 40 years a car with pop-ups was a promise, and the whir and blink when they opened was part of the deal. If you want to see the idea at its most beautiful, look at the FD in The One on the Wall.

Scale 1930–2010. The dashed line marks 2004, when the Esprit and the C5 Corvette ended production and pop-ups left volume production. Production years are widely published model-run dates; the Cord 810 was launched as a 1936 model and became the 812 for 1937.

Then they were gone. The last volume-production cars with pop-up headlights were the Lotus Esprit and the C5 Corvette, both of which ended production in 2004. Pedestrian-protection rules usually get the blame, but in Europe those rules only came into force in 2005, after the last pop-ups had already left. What really retired them was plastic. Once a headlight could be molded into any shape the body needed, there was no reason to hide it, and no reason to pay for the motors, linkages and weight that hiding it cost. Pop-ups aren't banned today. They're just very hard to bring back, and every concept car that tries gets a standing ovation from people over 40.

1962–2014A Brighter Kind of Fire

The next major changes happened inside the lamp, and they changed the color of the night. Halogen glows warm, a soft gold. In the autumn of 1991 BMW gave the E32 750iL the first xenon headlamps in series production, Bosch's Litronic system, on the low beam only and at first only on the V12 cars. Xenon, also called high-intensity discharge or HID, has no filament at all. A pulse of up to 25,000 volts strikes an arc between 2 electrodes inside a small capsule of gas, and the light that comes out is whiter, bluer and far more efficient. Other drivers noticed immediately. For a decade, that cold blue-white flash in the mirror meant something expensive had come up behind you. BMW brought xenon to America in 1993.

LEDs took away the last of the filament. Audi's A8 W12 became the first series-production car with LED daytime running lights at the end of 2003. In May 2007 the Lexus LS 600h hybrid became the first car with LED low beams, made by Koito. Then in 2008 the Audi R8 offered the first headlamp that did every job with LEDs, 54 of them in each lamp, and it was standard on the V10. By Audi's figures those LEDs made about 100 lumens of light for every watt of electricity, already beating xenon's roughly 80, which was itself about 4 times as efficient as halogen.

LEDs did something more important than save power. They were tiny, they lit instantly and they could be arranged in any pattern, so the headlight became a signature. A strip of daytime running lights now tells you the brand from down the block, long before you can read a badge. Audi went further in 2013 with Matrix LED headlights on the A8: 25 high-beam LEDs in each lamp, any of which a camera could switch off to cut a dark notch around another car while the rest of the road stayed lit. These technologies overlapped rather than replacing one another overnight, and in 2014 lasers joined them. BMW delivered its first i8s with laser lights in June 2014, and Audi says its R8 LMX was the first production car with laser high beams. Both companies spent that year claiming the same first, which may be the most glorious argument 2 lighting departments have ever had.

1983–todayThe Face Behind the Plastic

None of that would have looked like anything if the lens had stayed glass. Another turning point came in 1983, when US regulations permitted headlighting systems with replaceable bulbs. Unlike standardized sealed beams, these systems had no prescribed overall dimensions, which gave designers freedom over shape for the first time in 43 years. Ford had a car waiting. The 1984 Lincoln Continental Mark VII arrived with flush, aerodynamic composite headlamps, the first on an American car since before the war, and it didn't take long for nearly every car and truck sold here to follow.

Lincoln did it again a decade later. In 1995 the Mark VII's successor, the Mark VIII, offered xenon headlamps on its LSC version, the first time an American-built car had them.

Aerodynamic composite headlights followed everywhere. Plastic allowed shapes and styling freedom that glass couldn't readily provide, and headlights became part of the bodywork instead of holes cut into it. That also gave cars expressions, and expressions can start arguments. The Porsche 996's headlamps earned the nickname "fried eggs," and they were controversial enough that Porsche reshaped them at the facelift; the car underneath deserved better, as The Unsung Hero argues at length.

A modern clear outer lens should also be distinguished from an additional cover placed over a finished headlamp. In a 1996 interpretation, NHTSA explained that its limits on separate covers and grilles were there to preserve the lamp's tested performance, including its protection against deterioration from scratching, moisture and environmental exposure.

Plastic brought a maintenance tradeoff of its own. Ultraviolet light and road grit leave polycarbonate lenses cloudy or yellow, and anyone who has looked closely at the front of an older car has seen it. In a limited 2018 study using headlights from 2 sedans about 11 years old, AAA found that the deteriorated lamps delivered only 22% of the low-beam light of new original-equipment assemblies. Restoring them brought the output back to about 70%. Aftermarket replacements reached 83% to 90% but fell short on some intensity requirements and were more likely to throw glare, and only new original-equipment lamps got back to 100%. The result applied to the lamps AAA tested, but it shows how much the condition of the outer lens matters.

1937–1993Yellow Nights and Swedish Winters

For 56 years, the most famous headlight rule in Europe had nothing to do with brightness. It was about color. A French decree of November 3, 1936 required cars registered in France to shine selective yellow light, new cars from April 1937 and every car on the road by 1939. Yellow fog lamps were allowed across Europe, but France was the only country that demanded yellow headlights, so for more than half a century a pair of golden lights coming toward you on a European road almost always meant a French car. Drive a Citroën DS through a wet night with its original yellow lamps and you understand why people still miss them. The light looks warm, the rain looks softer, and the whole scene could have been filmed in 1962.

Nobody has ever been entirely sure why. The official arguments were less glare and less fatigue for drivers at night. A study published by La Documentation Française says the decree came at the request of the military, without saying what the military wanted. The popular story, that yellow lights let the French tell their cars from German ones in wartime, doesn't hold up, because the rule came before the war did.

Then there's the fog, which is what most people think yellow light is for. The theory is that yellow light, with its longer wavelength, scatters less than blue and so reaches farther through fog. That's true for particles much smaller than a wave of light, which is why the sky is blue. Fog droplets are enormous by comparison, and as the lighting researcher John Bullough told The Drive, color makes almost no difference to how water droplets scatter light. Yellow doesn't punch through fog any better than white. What it does is remove the blue end of the spectrum, which the eye finds hardest to handle and which feeds the sensation of glare, so the same fog can feel calmer through yellow. That comfort is real. It just isn't the same thing as seeing farther.

The price of the color was light. Filtering out the blue cost a lamp about 15% of its output, and when the Dutch road-safety institute SWOV reviewed the evidence in 1976 it concluded that yellow and white headlamps were equivalent for safety, though yellow caused less discomfort glare. France kept its rule anyway until January 1, 1993, when white headlights became legal again and it fell into line with its neighbors. A government answer to the National Assembly at the time noted that France was the only country still requiring yellow, and that yellow lamps cost more than white ones.

The color refused to die. Selective yellow fog lamps are still legal on both sides of the Atlantic. Le Mans turned the old road rule into a racing tradition, eventually keeping yellow headlights for its slower GT cars, and BMW's CS and CSL models wear yellow-tinted lights as a tribute to GT racing. The French rule lasted 56 years, and in its way it still hasn't ended.

Sweden fought the same darkness from the other direction. Its winters are long and its daylight thin, and Saab treated being seen as seriously as seeing. From the 1971 model year the Saab 99 came with headlamp wipers and washers, a world first, and Sweden later made them compulsory on new cars. Then, on October 1, 1977, Sweden became the first country to require every motor vehicle to drive with its lights on in daylight, all year round. Look at almost any new car's front end today and you can see that Swedish idea glowing in the middle of the afternoon.

1967–todayLight That Thinks

Headlights began responding to the car's movement long before cars began driving themselves. Beverly tried it in 1904 and Tucker in 1948, but the version that stuck came from Citroën. From 1967 the DS offered inner headlamps linked to the steering, turning into bends to light the road ahead of the car rather than the trees beyond it. Drive one at night on a winding road and you understand the DS in a single corner, which is a big part of why The Goddess of Serenity exists. America didn't share the enthusiasm. According to the Citroën enthusiasts' site Citroënvie, from January 1, 1971 any new Citroën brought into the US or Canada had to make do with fixed lamps and no glass in front of them, and the DS and SM lost their best trick at the border.

Modern adaptive driving beams take that idea much further by reshaping the light around other traffic. A camera watches the road, and the lamp keeps the high beam on everywhere except around the other cars, which sit in a moving tunnel of shade. In February 2022 NHTSA announced a rule permitting systems that meet US performance requirements, allowing more illumination where it's useful while limiting glare toward other drivers. Strict test requirements kept them rare here compared with Europe and Asia, AutoGuide reported. On October 6, 2026, NHTSA said it would rewrite Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 108, the lighting rule, using negotiated rulemaking for the first time in more than 25 years. The agenda covers glare from modern headlights, LEDs and automatic high beams, how high headlamps sit and where they aim, tests for plastic lenses and closer alignment with international standards, with comments due November 9.

The high beam with a hole in it

How an adaptive driving beam keeps the road lit without dazzling the oncoming driver

Adaptive on. The camera finds the oncoming car and switches off only the segments that would hit it. Everything else stays on high beam, so you see the shoulder, the sign and whatever is standing beside the road.

Simplified. Real systems use dozens to thousands of segments; Audi's first Matrix LED lamps used 25 high-beam LEDs per side.

The ratings drivers can actually look up are newer than you'd think. The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety published its first headlight ratings in 2016, and of the 82 headlight systems on 31 midsize cars it tested, exactly 1 earned a Good rating. The ratings changed behavior. IIHS research has since found that vehicles with Good-rated headlights have 19% fewer nighttime single-vehicle crashes and 23% fewer nighttime pedestrian crashes than vehicles with Poor ones, and the share of tested systems that threw excessive glare fell from 21% for the 2017 model year to 5% for 2026. More light was never the whole answer. Better-aimed light was.

Side note · Instrument lighting

The Glow on Your Side of the Glass

Headlights light the road. Everything else that glows in a car at night is aimed at you, and for a long time the best carmakers understood that it should glow as softly as possible. Climb into a BMW from the 1970s through the mid-2010s after dark and the instruments look back in a warm orange-red, a glow that goes back as far as the E9 coupes. People usually call it red. It's really an orange, which BMW enthusiast sites put at about 605 nanometers. Audi went deeper, lighting the dash and most of its instruments in a dark red. And Saab, the company that also built fighter jets, lit its instruments in a signature green.

Audi
deep red, dash and dials
BMW
orange-red, about 605 nm
Saab
green, and a Night Panel button
Today
white screens, edge to edge

The reasoning was sound. The rods in your eyes, the cells that do most of the work in the dark, are relatively insensitive to red light, so a dim red or orange glow lets you read a gauge without wrecking the night vision you need for the road. Submarine control rooms and aircraft cockpits used red light for exactly that reason, and that softer glow really does help your eyes settle back onto the darkness ahead. The catch is that red also makes fine print harder to read, especially for older eyes, which is one reason many cockpits have since moved to very dim white or blue-green lighting. BMW's orange looks like a compromise between the 2, and BMW itself has said its research found less difference between white and orange-red at night than it expected, so its newer cars light their displays in dimmed white. Every source agrees on the part that matters most: whatever the color, a dim panel protects your night vision and a bright one doesn't.

Saab took that idea further than anyone. In 1993 the new 900 introduced the Black Panel, renamed Night Panel from 1999: press a button and every instrument goes dark except the speedometer, with the other gauges and warnings coming back to life only when they need your attention. Saab called it "a good example of our aircraft heritage," and few features have aged better.

And then the screens arrived. The Mercedes MBUX Hyperscreen, launched on the EQS, spreads 3 displays under a single curved sheet of glass 141 cm (55.5 in) wide, and Cadillac's Escalade has a 38-inch curved display. Add ambient lighting in every color of the rainbow and the cabin of a modern luxury car at night looks less like a cockpit and more like Las Vegas seen from the air. Most of these cars have a night mode, and it's worth finding. Saab's idea, that the best instrument panel at night is the one you can barely see, is still the right one.

What comes nextTalking to the Street

That progression provides a useful backdrop to lighting on self-driving vehicles. For more than a century, engineers have worked on helping people see from inside a car, and on keeping that light out of everyone else's eyes. Now the car has started needing to say something to the people outside it. When Mercedes' Drive Pilot is in control, approved cars can show turquoise marker lights in their headlamps, taillamps and mirrors, a color chosen under an SAE recommendation because nothing else on the road uses it. In late 2023 California allowed them on test cars and Nevada allowed them on production EQS and S-Class models from the 2026 model year, the first approvals of their kind anywhere.

It's a small light with a large job. The first headlights told the driver where the road went. The next ones may have to tell everyone else who's driving. As automated vehicles develop, lighting raises an additional design question: how can people outside the car understand what it is doing? The answer, as it has been since the first match met the first acetylene burner, will come in light.

Somewhere tonight, on a road with no streetlights, a pair of headlights will reach around a bend before the car does. That moment hasn't changed in 130 years. Everything that makes it possible has.
